About.Name: Drew Fleming
About.AboutText: Hi, I’m Andrew Fleming. I’m an electrical engineering student at Seattle Pacific University with a strong interest in power systems, renewable energy, and how electrical infrastructure supports real communities. I enjoy working on projects where I can design and build something tangible, whether that’s an energy system, a control setup, or a hands on prototype that solves a real problem. I like learning new tools as I go and figuring things out through testing and iteration. Much of my best work has come from collaborating with classmates and talking through ideas until the system starts to make sense. Outside of class, I’m often working on side projects or helping friends with their builds, and I value staying curious, growing my skills, and taking every opportunity to learn something new.

Experience.ExperienceText: I have grown a lot by taking on projects that stretch me, especially my current work building a small-scale airborne wind generator for my senior design project. It has pushed my skills in power systems, controls, and real hands on problem solving. I am wrapping up my final year and getting ready to step into a career in sustainable energy, confident in the work I have done and the direction I am heading.
Experience.EducationText: I am a senior Electrical Engineering student at Seattle Pacific University, minoring in Appropriate and Sustainable Engineering. My coursework in electronics, signals, and microgrids has shaped how I approach real engineering problems, and my roles as a Lead Resident Advisor and IEEE Vice President have strengthened my communication and leadership. My studies also led me into airborne wind energy research, which I am continuing through my small scale airborne wind generator project.

Project1.Title: Personal Weather Probe
Project1.Desc: For my Junior Design project, I designed and built an autonomous water weather probe using a Raspberry Pi Pico as the main controller to collect temperature data at multiple depths in real environmental conditions. The system used two motor driven mechanisms, one to deploy a permanent anchor that held the device in place and a second to lower and raise a temperature sensor probe up to 15 feet, while the Pico coordinated motor control, sensor readings, and data logging to an SD card. The probe was powered by a 12 V battery supported by solar panels that could either recharge the battery or supply power directly depending on system demand, and a major challenge was designing the electronics and wiring to be fully waterproof while remaining reliable and serviceable, which ultimately gave me valuable experience in autonomous system design, embedded control, and environmental engineering.

Project2.Title: Laser Tag Blasters
Project2.Desc:
For my microcontroller systems course, I designed and built a pair of fully functional laser tag blasters using a Raspberry Pi Pico as the main controller. Each blaster transmitted an infrared signal and used IR receivers to detect hits from another player. I programmed the system in C++ and implemented a lockout safety feature that required the buttons to be pressed in a specific sequence before the blaster could activate, preventing accidental firing during startup.

The electronics combined off-the-shelf modules with custom tuning. I added external resistors and capacitors to condition and stabilize the IR transmitter and receiver circuits, improving detection reliability and reducing false triggers. I also integrated a small speaker that provided immediate feedback by buzzing when a player fired or successfully hit an opponent.

One of the biggest challenges was tuning the IR system so that hits were detected consistently without interference from ambient light or cross-talk between blasters. Debugging this required iterative testing, timing adjustments in software, and hardware refinements. The final result was a fun, interactive system that pulled together embedded programming, circuit design, and hands-on troubleshooting into a complete working product.

Project3.Title: PCB Design
Project3.Desc: I designed and built a custom dual adjustable linear power supply as a lab tool, taking the project from concept through fabrication and testing. The supply provides fixed outputs of 5 V, ±12 V, and ±30 V, along with a fully adjustable output ranging from 3–30 V, allowing it to support a wide range of bench and prototyping needs. The design process was intentionally end-to-end. I began by modeling the full circuit in Multisim, then validated the design on a breadboard to confirm voltage regulation and stability before committing to a PCB. I created the complete schematic and board layout in Altium, selected all components, and carefully routed both the power and control sections with attention to safe voltage spacing and linear regulation stability. After fabrication, I assembled and soldered the entire board by hand and verified correct operation across all output rails. This project gave me hands-on experience translating a theoretical design into a reliable physical system and reinforced the importance of iteration, testing, and layout decisions in power electronics.
